This is the construction guide for the data-generating processes behind the
[balancing reproduction](vignettes/balancing-reproduction.qmd). That vignette
answers *how the estimators perform*. This page answers the more basic question:
*what is each DGP, and how do I actually draw it with `pypanelsim`?*

The report contains **12 statistically distinct settings** across five DGP
families. Its results contain 14 named cases because each of the two
synthetic-control settings is fitted once with ridge unit balancing and once
with penalized-SCM unit balancing. Those are estimator choices, not four
different DGPs. The archived package also contains a sixth,
factor--synthetic mixture, which was not used in the 398-cell comparison; it is
documented and plotted here as well.

## Setup and the shared experiment

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pypanelsim as pps

config = pps.CanonicalPanelConfig(
    n_control=160,
    n_treated=40,
    n_pre=40,
    n_post=10,
    effect_slope=0.2,
    noise_variance=0.36,
)
config
```

Every factory on this page uses that configuration by default. Thus each draw
has 200 units by 50 periods. Units 0--159 are never treated; units 160--199
adopt at zero-based period 40. The treatment effect on every treated unit is
the deterministic ramp

$$
\tau_{it}=0.2(t-39),\qquad t=40,\ldots,49,
$$

so treated-period effects run from 0.2 through 2.0 and the true ATT is 1.1.
Independent observation noise has standard deviation 0.6. Only the untreated
outcome law changes across the sections below.

There are two equivalent ways to use a canonical DGP. The `*_design` form
returns a reusable simulator; the shorter form draws one panel immediately.

```{python}
# Reusable simulator: use this for Monte Carlo work.
simulator = pps.classic_factor_design(overlap=1.0, config=config)
panel_17 = simulator.simulate(seed=17)
panel_18 = simulator.simulate(seed=18)

# One-draw convenience function: same result for the same seed.
same_panel = pps.classic_factor(overlap=1.0, config=config, seed=17)
np.array_equal(panel_17.outcome, same_panel.outcome)
```

Each returned `PanelDataset` exposes `(unit, time)` arrays named `outcome`,
`treatment`, `untreated_outcome`, and `treatment_effect`. The plots below put
the observed outcome $Y$ and assignment $W$ side by side. The horizontal
boundary separates controls from treated units; the vertical boundary is the
common adoption date.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting helper"
def matshow_panels(draws, *, title, n_pre=config.n_pre):
    """Plot a sequence of (label, PanelDataset) pairs on a common Y scale."""
    scale = np.quantile(
        np.abs(np.concatenate([panel.outcome.ravel() for _, panel in draws])),
        0.98,
    )
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        len(draws),
        2,
        figsize=(11.5, 2.45 * len(draws)),
        squeeze=False,
        constrained_layout=True,
    )
    for row, (label, panel) in enumerate(draws):
        treated_boundary = panel.control_units.size - 0.5
        y_axis, w_axis = axes[row]
        y_axis.matshow(
            panel.outcome,
            aspect="auto",
            cmap="RdBu_r",
            vmin=-scale,
            vmax=scale,
        )
        w_axis.matshow(
            panel.treatment,
            aspect="auto",
            cmap="Greys",
            vmin=0,
            vmax=1,
        )
        for axis in (y_axis, w_axis):
            axis.axvline(n_pre - 0.5, color="#f5a623", linewidth=1.2)
            axis.axhline(treated_boundary, color="#f5a623", linewidth=1.2)
            axis.xaxis.set_ticks_position("bottom")
            axis.set_xlabel("period")
        y_axis.set_ylabel(f"{label}\nunit")
        y_axis.set_title("Observed outcome Y")
        w_axis.set_title("Treatment W")
    fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=14)
    plt.show()
```

## Construction map

This table is the shortest map from the original experiment labels to the
current reusable factories. Add the listed parameters, then call
`.simulate(seed=s)`. The corresponding one-draw function has the same name
without the `_design` suffix.

| Original family | Reusable factory | Parameter grid in the report |
|---|---|---|
| Classic factor | `classic_factor_design` | `overlap = 0, 1` |
| Weak factor | `weak_factor_design` | `overlap = 0, 1` |
| Mixed factor | `mixed_factor_design` | `overlap = 0, 1` |
| Synthetic control | `synthetic_control_design` | `active_share = 0.1, 0.5` |
| Time series | `time_series_design` | `coefficient = 0.2, 0.9`; `integrated = False, True` |
| Factor--synthetic | `factor_synthetic_design` | Archived; not in the 398-cell grid |

The same factories are available by name when a program chooses the design at
runtime:

```{python}
simulator = pps.make_canonical("time_series", coefficient=0.9, integrated=True)
panel = simulator.simulate(seed=202)
print(pps.available_canonical_designs())
```

## 1. Classic factor

Use this design for an interactive-fixed-effects panel with two strong,
drifting common factors:

$$
Y_{it}(0)=\lambda_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{it},
\qquad
\lambda_i\sim
\begin{cases}
N(-a,I_2),&i\text{ control},\\
N(a,I_2),&i\text{ treated}.
\end{cases}
$$

Each $f_t$ is a standardized AR(1) path with coefficient 0.5 plus a linear
drift $0.5t$. `overlap=0` gives the treated and control loadings the same
distribution. `overlap=1` moves their means to opposite sides of factor space,
making the treated counterfactual harder to recover from controls.

```{python}
classic_draws = [
    ("a = 0: overlapping loadings", pps.classic_factor(overlap=0, seed=110)),
    ("a = 1: separated loadings", pps.classic_factor(overlap=1, seed=110)),
]
matshow_panels(classic_draws, title="Classic factor DGP")
```

The realized latent objects are available for diagnosis:

```{python}
classic = classic_draws[1][1]
print("loadings:", classic.metadata["outcome"]["loadings"].shape)
print("factors:", classic.metadata["outcome"]["factors"].shape)
print("true ATT:", classic.true_att)
```

## 2. Weak factor

Use this to make the factor structure diffuse and individually weak. The law
is again $Y_{it}(0)=\lambda_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{it}$, but there are ten
factors: five drifting paths and five cycles
$\sin(\pi t/15)$. Every standardized factor is multiplied by 0.2. The same
`overlap` parameter controls the treated--control loading gap.

```{python}
weak_draws = [
    ("a = 0: overlapping loadings", pps.weak_factor(overlap=0, seed=120)),
    ("a = 1: separated loadings", pps.weak_factor(overlap=1, seed=120)),
]
matshow_panels(weak_draws, title="Weak-factor DGP")
```

```{python}
weak = weak_draws[0][1]
factor_sd = weak.metadata["outcome"]["factors"].std(axis=1, ddof=1)
print("number of factors:", factor_sd.size)
print("sample SD of every factor:", np.round(factor_sd, 3))
```

## 3. Mixed factor

Use this when one factor model is not shared by the whole population. The 200
units are split into two 100-unit blocks:

- the first block contains 60 controls and all 40 treated units and follows two
  drift factors;
- the second block contains 100 controls only and follows two cyclical factors.

The two blocks restart from the same RNG state, matching the archived
implementation. `overlap` separates treated loadings from the controls in the
first block. It does not turn overlap into a treatment-assignment probability.

```{python}
mixed_draws = [
    ("a = 0: overlap in drift block", pps.mixed_factor(overlap=0, seed=130)),
    ("a = 1: separated in drift block", pps.mixed_factor(overlap=1, seed=130)),
]
matshow_panels(mixed_draws, title="Mixed-factor DGP")
```

```{python}
mixed = mixed_draws[0][1]
outcome_meta = mixed.metadata["outcome"]
print("drift-block controls:", outcome_meta["first_group_controls"].size)
print("cyclical-block controls:", outcome_meta["second_group_controls"].size)
print("treated units:", mixed.treated_units.size)
```

## 4. Sparse synthetic control

Use this when treated counterfactuals are convex combinations of a sparse set
of donors. Control outcomes first follow a two-drift-factor model. Let
$m=\lceil qN_0\rceil$, where `q=active_share`. Controls with the $m$ largest
loading scores get sampling weight 1 and all other controls get weight 0.1.
Then $m$ donors are sampled without replacement and receive equal convex
weights:

$$
Y_{it}(0)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j\in\mathcal A}Y_{jt}^{\text{factor}}
+u_{it}+\varepsilon_{it},\qquad i\text{ treated}.
$$

The favored controls are *more likely* to be donors; the active set is not
simply the exact top-$m$ set. `active_share=0.1` gives 16 donors and
`active_share=0.5` gives 80 under the default configuration.

```{python}
synthetic_draws = [
    ("q = 0.1: 16 active donors", pps.synthetic_control(active_share=0.1, seed=140)),
    ("q = 0.5: 80 active donors", pps.synthetic_control(active_share=0.5, seed=140)),
]
matshow_panels(synthetic_draws, title="Sparse synthetic-control DGP")
```

```{python}
for label, draw in synthetic_draws:
    metadata = draw.metadata["outcome"]
    positive_weights = metadata["control_donor_weights"][
        metadata["control_donor_weights"] > 0
    ]
    print(label, "->", metadata["active_donors"].size,
          "donors; unique positive weight", np.unique(positive_weights))
```

The ridge and penalized-SCM rows in the report reuse these same two panel laws.
For example, both `synth_active01` and `synth_active01_penscm` call
`pps.synthetic_control(active_share=0.1, seed=seed)`; only the estimator's unit
loss changes afterward.

## 5. Time series

Use this when independent unit dynamics, rather than shared factors or donors,
generate untreated outcomes. For each unit,

$$
x_{it}=\phi x_{i,t-1}+\mu_i+\eta_{it},\qquad
\mu_i=0\ \text{for controls},\quad \mu_i=0.25\ \text{for treated units}.
$$

With `integrated=False`, $Y_{it}(0)=x_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}$. With
`integrated=True`, $Y_{it}(0)=\sum_{s\leq t}x_{is}+\varepsilon_{it}$, an
ARIMA(1,1,0)-type path. The report crosses low or high persistence
`coefficient=0.2, 0.9` with stationary or integrated paths.

```{python}
time_draws = [
    ("phi = 0.2, stationary", pps.time_series(coefficient=0.2, integrated=False, seed=150)),
    ("phi = 0.2, integrated", pps.time_series(coefficient=0.2, integrated=True, seed=150)),
    ("phi = 0.9, stationary", pps.time_series(coefficient=0.9, integrated=False, seed=150)),
    ("phi = 0.9, integrated", pps.time_series(coefficient=0.9, integrated=True, seed=150)),
]
matshow_panels(time_draws, title="Time-series DGP")
```

The outcome metadata records both choices and the process before observation
noise:

```{python}
integrated = time_draws[-1][1]
{
    key: integrated.metadata["outcome"][key]
    for key in ("coefficient", "integrated")
}
```

## 6. Factor--synthetic mixture

This archived design is useful even though it is not one of the 12 unique
settings in the final balancing grid. It forms one drift factor and one
cyclical factor, constructs a synthetic component using 40 active donors, and
then mixes the two signals equally:

$$
Y_{it}(0)=0.5Y_{it}^{\text{factor}}+0.5Y_{it}^{\text{SCM}}
+\varepsilon_{it}.
$$

The treated-specific noise in the SCM component has standard deviation 2.
`overlap` controls factor-loading separation exactly as in the other factor
designs.

```{python}
factor_synthetic_draws = [
    ("a = 0: overlapping loadings", pps.factor_synthetic(overlap=0, seed=160)),
    ("a = 1: separated loadings", pps.factor_synthetic(overlap=1, seed=160)),
]
matshow_panels(factor_synthetic_draws, title="Factor--synthetic mixture DGP")
```

## The exact report case dictionary

This is a self-contained version of the case map used by the balancing runner.
If the goal is to reproduce that experiment rather than choose one design
interactively, copy this dictionary.

```{python}
REPORT_DGPS = {
    "classic_a0": (pps.classic_factor_design, {"overlap": 0.0}),
    "classic_a1": (pps.classic_factor_design, {"overlap": 1.0}),
    "weak_a0": (pps.weak_factor_design, {"overlap": 0.0}),
    "weak_a1": (pps.weak_factor_design, {"overlap": 1.0}),
    "mixed_a0": (pps.mixed_factor_design, {"overlap": 0.0}),
    "mixed_a1": (pps.mixed_factor_design, {"overlap": 1.0}),
    "time_a02_i0": (pps.time_series_design, {"coefficient": 0.2, "integrated": False}),
    "time_a02_i1": (pps.time_series_design, {"coefficient": 0.2, "integrated": True}),
    "time_a09_i0": (pps.time_series_design, {"coefficient": 0.9, "integrated": False}),
    "time_a09_i1": (pps.time_series_design, {"coefficient": 0.9, "integrated": True}),
    "synth_active01": (pps.synthetic_control_design, {"active_share": 0.1}),
    "synth_active05": (pps.synthetic_control_design, {"active_share": 0.5}),
}

# Build reusable simulators once, then vary only the seed.
simulators = {
    name: factory(config=config, **parameters)
    for name, (factory, parameters) in REPORT_DGPS.items()
}
replication_37 = {
    name: simulator.simulate(seed=37)
    for name, simulator in simulators.items()
}

pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "case": name,
            "shape": panel.shape,
            "treated": panel.treated_units.size,
            "adoption period": np.unique(panel.adoption_times[panel.ever_treated]).item(),
            "true ATT": panel.true_att,
        }
        for name, panel in replication_37.items()
    ]
)
```

To obtain the runner's 14 case names, alias the two synthetic DGPs and attach
the different estimator configuration separately:

```{python}
ESTIMATOR_ONLY_CASES = {
    "synth_active01_penscm": ("synth_active01", "penalized_scm"),
    "synth_active05_penscm": ("synth_active05", "penalized_scm"),
}
```

## Mapping the original R generator

The canonical factories are named presets extracted from the original generic
`gen.simdata()` function. This is the parameter map for the presets used in the
balancing study:

| Original argument or label | `pypanelsim` equivalent |
|---|---|
| `N = 200`, `N.tr = 40` | `CanonicalPanelConfig(n_control=160, n_treated=40)` |
| `TT = 50`, `T.post = 10` | `CanonicalPanelConfig(n_pre=40, n_post=10)` |
| `eff.size = 0.2`, cumulative effect | `effect_slope=0.2` and `LinearRampEffect` |
| `error.noise = 0.6` | `noise_variance=0.36` |
| treated/control loading means `a` and `-a` | `overlap=a` |
| `num.active / N.co` | `active_share` |
| `ar.coef` | `coefficient` |
| integration order `I = 0, 1` | `integrated=False, True` |
| factor, time-series, SCM mixture weights | choose the named factory above |

This API reproduces the experiment presets and their NumPy draw order; it is
not a one-to-one wrapper around every possible mixture accepted by the generic
R function. In particular, arbitrary factor/time-series/SCM/fixed-effect
weights, arbitrary covariate arrays, and arbitrary donor weights should be
assembled with the composable `PanelSimulator` API. The preset that combines
factor and SCM components is `factor_synthetic_design`, with a fixed 50/50
mixture.

R and NumPy use different random-number generators, so the same integer seed is
not expected to produce cell-identical R and Python panels. The probability
laws, dimensions, and simulation-index convention are the reproduction target.

## Which design should I use?

| If you want to stress-test... | Start with... | Turn the difficulty knob... |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive fixed effects | `classic_factor_design()` | `overlap=1` |
| Many weak latent factors | `weak_factor_design()` | `overlap=1` |
| Population-specific factor structure | `mixed_factor_design()` | `overlap=1` |
| Sparse donor reconstruction | `synthetic_control_design()` | reduce `active_share` |
| Persistence and stochastic trends | `time_series_design()` | `coefficient=0.9, integrated=True` |
| Simultaneous factor and donor structure | `factor_synthetic_design()` | `overlap=1` |

For estimator-ready reshaping, use `panel.as_long_dict()` or the adapters on
the [interoperability page](interoperability.qmd). For the complete estimator
experiment and its results, continue to the
[balancing reproduction](vignettes/balancing-reproduction.qmd).
